label: pr 2-ineq
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pr 2-ineq}
Let \(N\ge 1\), \(\mu>-1\) and  \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) be bounded
Lipschitz domains such that
\[
0\in \Omega_1\subset \Omega_2.
\]
For $i=1,2$, $\{ \lambda^{\ln,\mu}_{k}(\Omega_i)\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ denote the sequence of  eigenvalues for problem
(\ref{eq: 1.1}) with $\Omega=\Omega_i$.

Then  for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\),
\[
  \lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_1)\ge \lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_2).
\]

label: prop:energy-space

head: environment

label: Euv1
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the variational min--max characterization of the Dirichlet
eigenvalues. Denote
\begin{align}\label{Euv1}
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u)
    =\int_{\Omega}u(x)(-\Delta)^{\ln}u(x)\,dx
    +2\mu \int_{\Omega} \Big(\log\frac1{|x|}\Big) u(x)^2 \,dx.
\end{align}
By Proposition  \ref{prop:energy-space},  the embedding
\[
{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)
\]
is compact for \(\mu>-1\).
Then the eigenvalues admit the min--max characterization
\[
\lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
=
\min_{\substack{H\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)\\ \dim H=k}}
\max_{u\in H\setminus\{0\}}
\frac{{\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u)}
{\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2},
\qquad k\in\mathbb{N},
\]
with eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

Let
\[
R_\Omega(u)=\frac{{\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u)}{\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2}.
\]
Then we have that
\[
\lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
=
\min_{\substack{H\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)\\ \dim H=k}}
\max_{u\in H\setminus\{0\}} R_\Omega(u).
\]

Since \(\Omega_1\subset\Omega_2\), for \(u\in C_c^\infty(\Omega_1)\), we observe that   
\(u\in C_c^\infty(\Omega_2)\) and 
$$
\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega_2)}^2 =\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega_1)}^2,\qquad \ 
{\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega_2}(u,u)=
{\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega_1}(u,u).
$$
Then it yields that
\[
R_{\Omega_2}(u)=R_{\Omega_1}(u).
\]
By density of \(C_c^\infty(\Omega_1)\) in \({\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_1)\),  
                                                                                                                   
we note that if \(H\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_1)\) is a  \(k\)-dimensional
subspace, then \( H\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_2)\) is also \(k\)-dimensional and
\[
\max_{u\in H\setminus\{0\}} R_{\Omega_1}(u)
=
\max_{v\in H\setminus\{0\}} R_{\Omega_2}(v).
\]
Using the min--max formula for \(\Omega_2\), we obtain that
\begin{align*}
\lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_2)
 &=
\min_{\substack{W\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_2)\\ \dim W=k}}
\max_{v\in W\setminus\{0\}} R_{\Omega_2}(v)
\\&\le
\min_{\substack{H\subset {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_1)\\ \dim H=k}}\,
\max_{u\in H\setminus\{0\}} R_{\Omega_1}(u)
=\lambda_k^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega_1).
\end{align*}
This completes the proof.\hfill$\Box$

title: Definition
body_md:
Let \(N\ge 1\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be a measurable function such that
\[
  d_f(t):=\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N: |f(x)|>t\}\bigr|<+\infty
  \qquad\text{for every} \ t>0.
\]
Denote \(\omega_N=|B_1(0)|\). The  symmetric decreasing rearrangement
of \(f\) is the function \(f^\#:\mathbb{R}^N\to[0,\, +\infty]\) defined by
\[
  f^\#(x)= \inf\Bigl\{t\ge0:\ d_f(t)\le \omega_N |x|^N\Bigr\}, \qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^N.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
  \{x\in\mathbb{R}^N: f^\#(x)>t\}
  =
  B_{r(t)}(0),
  \qquad
  |B_{r(t)}(0)|=d_f(t),
\]
where \(B_{r(t)}(0)\) is the open ball centered at the origin with the same
measure as the superlevel set \(\{x:|f(x)|>t\}\).
head: environment

label: lm 2.1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm 2.1}
Let \(N\ge1\),   \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) be a bounded Lipschitz domain containing the origin, 
\(R>0\) satisfy that \(|B_R(0)|=|\Omega|\).  For 
 \(u\in {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)\), denote by \(u^\#\) the symmetric decreasing rearrangement.


Then
\[
  u^\#\in {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(B_R(0)).
\]
head: environment

label: eq 2.1-re
title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(u\in C_c^{\infty}(\Omega)\),  we have that
\[
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,0,\Omega}(u,u)<+\infty.
\]
For \(s\in(0,1)\), the classical P\'olya--Szeg\H{o} inequality for the
fractional Laplacian shows that
\[
  \|(-\Delta)^{s/2}u^\#\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2
  \le
  \|(-\Delta)^{s/2}u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2
\]
and then
\[
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat{u^\#}(\xi)|^2\,d\xi  \le
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi
  <+\infty,
\]
where \[
  \widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-\frac N2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}e^{-{\bf i}  x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx.
\]
Thus, we have that
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat{u^\#}(\xi)|^2\,d\xi- \|u^\#\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2
  \le
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi-\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2,
\]
since \[
 \|u^\#\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2= \|u^\#\|_{L^2(B_R(0))}^2 =
  \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2. \]
 By the fact that $$|\xi|^{2s}=1+2s\log|\xi|+O(s^2) \qquad {\rm for} \ \ \xi\not=0$$ and 
passing to the limit as \(s\to0^+\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq 2.1-re}
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,0,B_R(0)}(u^\#,u^\#)\le
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,0,\Omega}(u,u) <+\infty.
\end{equation}
Therefore, it holds that
\begin{equation}\label{eq 04}
  u^\#\in {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(B_R(0)).
\end{equation}

Since \(C_c^\infty(\Omega)\) is density in \({\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)\)  (see \cite{ChenWeth2019}), 
then (\ref{eq 04}) holds for any  \(u\in {\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)\)
via taking a sequence functions in \(C_c^\infty(\Omega)\) approaching to 
$u$ in ${\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$ if necessary.\hfill$\Box$
head: manual

label: lm 2.2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
When $f(u)=u$, this lemma is a standard consequence of the Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement inequality,
see \cite[Theorem 3.4]{Lieb1} or \cite[Theorem 368]{Hardy1}.  For the general increasing $f$, we provide the detailed  proof.


Set \(v:=f(u)\). Since \(f\) is strictly increasing and locally Lipschitz continuous, the superlevel sets of
\(v\) and \(u\) are related by
\[
  \{x\in\mathbb R^N: v(x)>t\}
  =
  \{x\in\mathbb R^N: u(x)>f^{-1}(t)\}
\]
for \(t\) in the range of \(f\). Hence
\[
  |\{x: v(x)>t\}|
  =
  |\{x: u(x)>f^{-1}(t)\}|.
\]
By definition of the symmetric decreasing rearrangement,
\[
  |\{x: u^\#(x)>s\}|=|\{x: u(x)>s\}|
  \qquad \text{for all } s\ge 0.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
  |\{x: f(u^\#(x))>t\}|
  &=
  |\{x: u^\#(x)>f^{-1}(t)\}|
  \\[1mm]&\ \, =
  |\{x: u(x)>f^{-1}(t)\}|
 \, =
  |\{x: v(x)>t\}|.
\end{align*}
Since \(f\) is increasing and \(u^\#\) is radially decreasing, the function
\(f(u^\#)\) is also radially decreasing. Thus \(f(u^\#)\) is the symmetric
decreasing rearrangement of \(v=f(u)\), i.e.
\[
  (f(u))^\# = f(u^\#).
\]

Now apply the Hardy--Littlewood rearrangement inequality to \(v=f(u)\).
For every \(t\ge 0\), let \({B_{r(t)}(0)}\subset\mathbb R^N\) be the ball centered at the
origin with
\[
  |{B_{r(t)}(0)}|=|\{x: v(x)>t\}|.
\]
Since \(w\) is radially increasing, among all sets of a fixed measure the
integral of \(w(|x|)\) is minimized by the centered ball. Hence
\[
  \int_{\{v>t\}} w(|x|)\,dx
  \;\ge\;
  \int_{B_{r(t)}(0)} w(|x|)\,dx.
\]
Using the layer-cake representation,
\[
  \int_{\mathbb R^N} w(|x|) f(u(x))\,dx
  =
  \int_{\mathbb R^N} w(|x|) v(x)\,dx
  =
  \int_0^\infty \int_{\{v>t\}} w(|x|)\,dx\,dt.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \int_{\mathbb R^N} w(|x|) f(u(x))\,dx
  &=
  \int_0^\infty \int_{\{v>t\}} w(|x|)\,dx\,dt \\[1mm]
  &\ge
  \int_0^\infty \int_{B_{r(t)}(0)} w(|x|)\,dx\,dt \\[1mm]
  &=
  \int_0^\infty \int_{\{v^\#>t\}} w(|x|)\,dx\,dt \\[1mm]
  &=
  \int_{\mathbb R^N} w(|x|) v^\#(x)\,dx \\[1mm]
  &=
  \int_{\mathbb R^N} w(|x|) f(u^\#(x))\,dx,
\end{aligned}
\]
which implies the inequality (\ref{inq 2.1}).

It remains to prove the equality case. Suppose equality holds in the above
chain. Then for almost every \(t\ge 0\),
\[
  \int_{\{v>t\}} w(|x|)\,dx
  =
  \int_{B_{r(t)}(0)} w(|x|)\,dx.
\]
Since \(w\) is strictly increasing, the only sets of a given measure for which
this equality can hold are, up to null sets, the centered balls. Hence
\[
  \{v>t\}={B_{r(t)}(0)}
  \qquad \text{up to a null set, for a.e. } t\ge 0.
\]
Thus
\[
  \mathbf 1_{\{v>t\}}(x)=\mathbf 1_{B_{r(t)}(0)}(x)
  \qquad \text{for a.e. } x\in\mathbb R^N,\ \text{for a.e. } t\ge 0.
\]
Integrating in \(t\), we get
\[
  v(x)
  =
  \int_0^\infty \mathbf 1_{\{v>t\}}(x)\,dt
  =
  \int_0^\infty \mathbf 1_{B_{r(t)}(0)}(x)\,dt
  =
  v^\#(x)
\]
for almost every \(x\in\mathbb R^N\). Hence \(v=v^\#\) a.e., i.e.
\[
  f(u)=f(u^\#)\quad\text{a.e. in } \mathbb R^N.
\]
Since \(f\) is strictly increasing, it is injective, and therefore
\[
  u=u^\#\quad\text{a.e. in } \mathbb R^N.
\]
Conversely, if \(u=u^\#\) a.e., then the two integrals are clearly equal.
The proof ends.
\hfill$\Box$
head: manual

label: lem:fourier-hardy
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:fourier-hardy}
Let $N\geq 1$ and  $u\in{\mathcal S}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be real-valued.
Then                                                                                 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-log}
 \widehat{(\log\frac1{|\cdot|})}(\xi)
  =
  \theta_N\,\mathrm{Pf}\frac{1}{|\xi|^N}
+
  \alpha_N\,\delta_0,
\end{equation}
where $ \theta_N=2^{\frac N2-1}\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac N2\bigr)>0$,
$\mathrm{Pf}\frac1{|\xi|^N}$ is the finite-part regularization of the
non-integrable function $|\xi|^{-N}$, defined by
\[
  \Bigl\langle \mathrm{Pf}\frac1{|\xi|^N},\,\varphi\Bigr\rangle
  =
  \int_{|\xi|\ge1}\frac{\varphi(\xi)}{|\xi|^N}\,d\xi
  +
  \int_{|\xi|<1}\frac{\varphi(\xi)-\varphi(0)}{|\xi|^N}\,d\xi,
  \qquad\forall\, \varphi\in{\mathcal S}(\mathbb{R}^N),
\]
and $\alpha_N$ is a constant depending only on $N$ and on the normalization of
the finite part.


                                                                                                          

Moreover, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hardy-fourier-form}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\big(\log\frac1{|x|}\big)\,u(x)^2\,dx
  =
  \theta_N
    \int_{|\xi|\ge1}\frac{\widehat{u^2}(\xi)}{|\xi|^N}\,d\xi
    +
    \theta_N\int_{|\xi|<1}\frac{\widehat{u^2}(\xi)-\widehat{u^2}(0)}{|\xi|^N}\,d\xi
  +
\alpha_N \|u\|_{2}^2,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\widehat{u^2}$ denotes the Fourier transform of the function $u^2$,
\[
  \widehat{u^2}(\xi)
  =
  (2\pi)^{-\frac {N}2}\, \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}e^{-{\bf i}x\cdot\xi}u(x)^2\,dx
  =
 \bigl(\widehat u*\widehat u\bigr)(\xi).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $0<\lambda<N$, the classical Riesz potential formula (see \cite{GS})
gives
\[
  \mathcal F\bigl[|\cdot|^{-\lambda}\bigr](\xi)
  =
  2^{\frac N2-\lambda}
  \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{N-\lambda}{2}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac\lambda2\bigr)}
  \,|\xi|^{\lambda-N}
  =:
  \theta_\lambda\,|\xi|^{\lambda-N}
\]
with
$$ \theta_\lambda=2^{\frac N2-\lambda}
  \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{N-\lambda}{2}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac\lambda2\bigr)}.$$
Since
$|x|^{-\lambda}=1-\lambda\log|x|+O(\lambda^2)$ as $\lambda\to0^+$, we have that
\[
  \mathcal F\bigl[|\cdot|^{-\lambda}\bigr]
  =
  (2\pi)^{\frac N2}\delta_0-\lambda\,\widehat{\log|\cdot|}+O(\lambda^2).
\]
Since $\Gamma(\lambda/2)=2/\lambda+\Gamma'(1)+O(\lambda)$ as $\lambda\to0^+$, one has
$\theta_\lambda=\lambda \theta_N+\tfrac12\lambda^2 \theta_N''+O(\lambda^3)$, where $\theta_N''=\frac{d}{d\lambda} \theta_\lambda\big|_{\lambda=0}$, while for $\varphi\in{\mathcal S}(\mathbb{R}^N)$,
\[
  \bigl\langle|\xi|^{\lambda-N},\varphi\bigr\rangle
  =
  \frac{|\mathbb S^{N-1}|}{\lambda}\,\varphi(0)
  +
  \Bigl\langle \mathrm{Pf}\frac1{|\xi|^N},\varphi\Bigr\rangle
  +
  o(1)
  \quad{\rm as}\ \,  \lambda\to0^+.
\]
                                                                                     
                                              
                                               
By the fact that $\theta_N|\mathbb S^{N-1}|=(2\pi)^{\frac N2}$, it yields
\[
  \widehat{(\log\frac1{|\cdot|})}(\xi)
  =
  \theta_N\,\mathrm{Pf}\frac1{|\xi|^N}
  +
 \alpha_N\,\delta_0
  \quad {\rm with}
\ \  \alpha_N=\frac{\theta_N''\,|\mathbb S^{N-1}|}{2},
\]
and then \eqref{eq:fourier-log} holds.

\smallskip

For $u\in{\mathcal S}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, one has $u^2\in{\mathcal S}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, and by Parseval's identity, we have that
\[
  \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(\log\frac1{|x|})\,u(x)^2\,dx
  =
  \Bigl\langle\log\frac1{|\cdot|},\,u^2\Bigr\rangle
  =
  \Bigl\langle
   \widehat{\log\frac1{|\cdot|}},\,\widehat{u^2}
  \Bigr\rangle .
\]
Combining with \eqref{eq:fourier-log} and the fact that
$$\widehat{u^2}=\widehat u*\widehat u,\qquad
\widehat{u^2}(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u(x)^2dx=\|u\|_{2}^2,$$
we obtain \eqref{eq:hardy-fourier-form}.
                              
                                                                           
                                                    
\hfill$\Box$
head: manual

label: eq:energy-decomp01a
title: Proof
body_md:
When $\mu=0$, the Faber--Krahn inequality
has been established in  \cite{ChenWeth2019} and  the rigidity  has been done  in \cite{CCH26}. So in the sequel, we only
deal with the case $\mu\in(-1,0)$. 



Recall that 
\begin{align}\label{eq:energy-decomp01a}
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u)
    =\int_{\Omega}u(x)(-\Delta)^{\ln}u(x)\,dx
    +2\mu \int_{\Omega} \Big(\log\frac1{|x|}\Big) u(x)^2 \,dx,
\end{align}
by \cite[Theorem 1.3]{LWY}, for $\mu>-1$,  we have that the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of 
the logarithmic Hardy operator $ {\mathcal L}_\mu$ could be given by
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  =
  \min\Bigl\{
    {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u):
    u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega),\ \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=1
  \Bigr\},
\]
and the minimum is attained by a positive eigenfunction
$\varphi_1^{\ln,\mu}\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)$. By Proposition \ref{prop:energy-space}, we note that 
$\varphi_1^{\ln,\mu}\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$ when $\mu>-1$.

 \smallskip


Let $R>0$ satisfy that $|B_R(0)|=|\Omega|$, for $u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$,
denote by $u^\#$  the symmetric decreasing rearrangement,
 then  $\|u^\#\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}=\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}$ and Lemma \ref{lm 2.1} implies that
$u^\#\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(B_R(0))$.


Now we claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symmetrization}
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu, B_R(0)}(u^\#,u^\#)
  \;\le\;
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u).
\end{equation}
where the equality holds if and only if $u^\#=u$ a.e. in $\mathbb{R}^N$. 
Indeed,  since  $\mu\in(-1,0)$,  then  $2\mu\log\frac1{|x|}$ is radially symmetric and  is strictly increasing about $|x|$
on $(0,\infty)$, then we apply Lemma \ref{lm 2.2} with $f(u)=u^2$ to obtain that
 $$2\mu \int_{B_R(0)}\log\frac1{|x|} u^\#(x)^2\,dx\leq 2\mu \int_{\Omega}\log\frac1{|x|} \,u(x)^2\,dx,  $$
which, combining (\ref{eq 2.1-re}), i.e.
$${\mathcal E}_{\ln,0, B_R(0)}(u^\#,u^\#)
  \;\le\;
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,0,\Omega}(u,u)$$
  implies that
 \eqref{eq:symmetrization}. \smallskip

 Therefore, we have that
\[
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(u,u)
  \;\ge\;
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu, B_R(0)}(u^\#,u^\#)
  \;\ge\;
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}\bigl(B_R(0)\bigr),
\]
since $u^\#$ is  admissible  for the ball $B_R(0)$ with
$\|u^\#\|_{L^2(B_R(0))}=1$. Taking the infimum over all $u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$
with $\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=1$ yields
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  \;\ge\;
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}\bigl(B_R(0)\bigr).
\]
                                

\smallskip
 Finally, we consider the equality case.
Assume $\lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)=\lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_R(0))$  and let
$\varphi_1:=\varphi_1^{\ln,\mu}\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$ be the positive first
eigenfunction of $\Omega$, normalized by
$\|\varphi_1\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=1$. Then
\begin{align*}
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  =
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,\Omega}(\varphi_1,\varphi_1)
  &\;\ge\;
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu, B_R(0)}(\varphi_1^\#,\varphi_1^\#)
 \\[1mm]& \;\ge\;
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}\bigl(B_R(0)\bigr)
  =
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega),
\end{align*}
hence all inequalities above are equalities.
 In particular, equality
holds in \eqref{eq:symmetrization} holds  only if
$\varphi_1=\varphi_1^\#$ almost everywhere in $\mathbb{R}^N$.



Conversely, equality
is trivial when $\Omega=B_R(0)$. Thus equality holds in
\eqref{eq:FK-small} if and only if  $\Omega=B_R(0)$..
\hfill$\Box$
head: manual
name: Theorem \refteo 1.2$(i)$

label: re1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{re1}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{teo 1.2} $(i)$, the ball
$B_R(0)$ minimizes the first eigenvalue among all domains of the same
volume, i.e.
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_R(0))
  =
  \min\Big\{
    \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega):
    \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N \text{ bounded Lipschitz},\ 0\in\Omega,\
    |\Omega|=|B_R(0)|
  \Big\},
\]
for every $V=|\Omega|>0$, and the minimum is attained exactly at the ball
centered at the origin.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Our aim is to construct a   Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ containing the origin, with
$|\Omega|=|B_R(0)|=V$   such that for  $\mu>0$,
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  <
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_R(0)).
\]

To this end,  we fix $V>0$ and let $R>0$ satisfy $|B_R(0)|=V$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ and
$r>0$ such that
\[
  |B_\varepsilon(0)|+|B_r(0)|<V .
\]
Let $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$ with $|x_0|$ large enough which will be chosen later. Connect the two balls
$B_\varepsilon(0)$ and $B_r(x_0)$ by a thin tube $T$ of volume
$V-|B_\varepsilon(0)|-|B_r(0)|$. Denote
\[
  \Omega=B_\varepsilon(0)\cup T\cup B_r(x_0).
\]
Then $\Omega$ is a bounded Lipschitz domain and satisfies that
 $$0\in\Omega,\quad |\Omega|=V=|B_R(0)|,\quad B_r(x_0)\subset\Omega.$$

Since $B_r(x_0)\subset\Omega$, every function
$u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(B_r(x_0))$,  we have that 
$u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(\Omega)$ and  the Rayleigh quotient for $\Omega$ is no
larger than the Rayleigh quotient for $B_r(x_0)$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:monotonicity-counter}
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  \le
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0)).
\end{equation}

We now estimate $\lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0))$ as $|x_0|\to+\infty$. Recall
that 
\begin{align}\label{1b0}
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu, B_r(x_0)}(u,u)
    =\int_{B_r(x_0)}u(x)(-\Delta)^{\ln}u(x)\,dx
    +2\mu \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \Big(\log\frac1{|x|}\Big) u(x)^2 \,dx,
\end{align}
For $x\in B_r(x_0)$ and $|x_0|>2r$, we have
\[
  \left|\log\frac1{|x|}-\log\frac1{|x_0|}\right|
  =
  \left|\log\frac{|x_0|}{|x|}\right|
  \le
  \log\frac{|x_0|}{|x_0|-r}
  \le
  \frac{2r}{|x_0|}.
\]
Thus, uniformly on $B_r(x_0)$,
\[
  2\mu\log\frac1{|x|}
  =
  2\mu\log\frac1{|x_0|}
  +
  O\!\left(\frac{\mu r}{|x_0|}\right).
\]
Combining with (\ref{1b0}), it yields that  for every $u\in{\mathbb H}_0^{\ln}(B_r(x_0))$,
\[
  {\mathcal E}_{\ln,\mu,B_r(x_0)}(u,u)
  =
  \int_{B_r(x_0)}u(x)(-\Delta)^{\ln}u(x)\,dx
  +
  2\mu\log\frac1{|x_0|}\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2
  +
  O\!\left(\frac{\mu r}{|x_0|}\right)\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2.
\]
Dividing by $\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2$ and taking the infimum over all admissible
$u$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:far-ball-asymptotic}
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0))
  =
  \lambda_1^{\ln,0}(B_r(x_0))
  +
  2\mu\log\frac1{|x_0|}
  +
  O\!\left(\frac{\mu r}{|x_0|}\right).
\end{equation}
Since $\mu>0$, then $2\mu\log\frac1{|x_0|}\to -\infty$ as
$|x_0|\to+\infty$ and
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0))
  \to
  -\infty
  \quad\text{as }\, |x_0|\to+\infty.
\]
Then we could choose $|x_0|$  large enough such that
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0))
  <
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_R(0)).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:monotonicity-counter}, we get
\[
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(\Omega)
  \le
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_r(x_0))
  <
  \lambda_1^{\ln,\mu}(B_R(0)).
\]
But $|\Omega|=V=|B_R(0)|$. Hence the Faber--Krahn inequality is
violated in this case of $\mu>0$. The proof ends.\hfill$\Box$
